summary: Responds to RFC 110 with new rules for using IBM 2741 terminals on the network. The author argues the earlier conventions were inconsistent and hard to use, and that some 2741 keyboards lack characters such as less-than, greater-than and vertical bar. The proposed conventions avoid them.

plainLanguage.summary: This note revises keying rules for using an IBM 2741 terminal on the network. A shared escape key lets users enter special functions and characters missing from one keyboard.

questions: how to avoid missing characters on a 2741 terminal
which keys does the correspondence 2741 lack
how did the 2741 enter missing characters
subtitle: Revised IBM 2741 keyboard conventions that avoid characters missing from one keyboard type.

tldr.problem: The author found RFC 110's conventions difficult to use and noted that a correspondence IBM 2741 keyboard lacks several characters used in them.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal assigns single keys to character escape and character delete, then uses the escape key followed by another key for other special functions and missing graphics.
tldr.outcome: RFC 135 proposes replacing the conventions in RFC 110. It focuses on making the conventions usable with the correspondence 2741 keyboard.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 135 as Unknown and records that it updates RFC 110. It is a proposal for terminal conventions, not a network-wide terminal standard.

sections.title: Why the Conventions Change
sections.content:
Wayne Hathaway proposes replacing the conventions in RFC 110 because he considers them inconsistent and difficult to use. The correspondence 2741 keyboard lacks less-than, greater-than, logical not, and vertical bar, so conventions that require those characters cannot support that keyboard.

The author weighs the convenience of a dedicated special-function key against the extra keystrokes needed to enter that character as ordinary data.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier rules depend on characters that one 2741 keyboard does not have. The proposal changes the rules so that keyboard can still be used.

sections.title: Escape and Special Functions
sections.content:
The proposed character escape is the cent sign, which the RFC says appears on both regular and correspondence 2741 terminals and is not in ASCII. Character delete uses the backspace key. Other special functions begin with the escape character and then use a defining key.

New functions include line continuation for a logical line that spans physical lines, and ASCII control for entering control characters by abbreviation.
sections.plainLanguage: The cent sign starts most special key combinations, and backspace deletes a character. A two-key form can also enter control characters by name.

sections.title: Entering Missing Graphics
sections.content:
The RFC gives two-key forms for graphics that do not appear on either 2741 keyboard, including brackets, braces, backslash, apostrophe, circumflex, and tilde. It also defines forms for entering the cent sign and backspace as ordinary data.

The author again warns that less-than and greater-than are absent from the correspondence keyboard and should not be used in the conventions.
sections.plainLanguage: When a needed character is missing, the user types the escape and a stand-in key. This lets the terminal represent characters without requiring the missing key.
